docs.text: HardFOC driver FDO2 Driver ¶ A C++17 driver for the PyroScience FDO2-G2 optical oxygen sensor. It identifies the module, measures oxygen partial pressure and temperature, reads the raw optical, pressure and humidity data and decodes the status and error codes, on any MCU with a UART. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub The driver has no platform code. You give it a small class that writes bytes to a UART and returns one reply line; it does the rest: the ASCII commands, reply parsing, unit scaling, status bits and #ERRO codes. Optical oxygen sensor module FDO2-G2 PyroScience Measures Oxygen partial pressure 0 to 1000 hPa (0 to 100 % O 2 at 1013 mbar), plus temperature, pressure and humidity inside the housing Accuracy ±5 hPa at 200 hPa (10 °C to 40 °C); response time t 63 under 2 s Host interface UART, 3.0 V levels (3.3 V absolute maximum), 19200 baud 8N1 after power-up, ASCII commands Supply 3.3 V to 5.0 V DC (5.5 V absolute maximum); about 8 mA standby, 40 mA peak Connector Molex 560020-0420, four pins: GND, TXD, RXD, VCC Driver uses #VERS , #IDNR , #MOXY , #MRAW , #LOGO ; no command that writes the module's flash Datasheet (v5, 03/2026) What you get ¶ One object per sensor. fdo2::Driver<YourUart> sends a command and returns a typed result. See API guide . Engineering units. hPa, °C, mbar, mV and %RH, scaled from the module's integer fields, and volume percent O 2 from the internal pressure sensor. See UART protocol . Status you cannot miss. Every reading carries the status word, and MoxyStatusOkForOxygen() applies the datasheet's rule. See API guide . Blocking or split. MeasureMoxy() waits for the reply; SendMeasure() and TryReadReplyLine() let a loop serve other devices during the measurement. See API guide . Zero-overhead portability. The port is a CRTP class with three methods: no virtual calls, no heap, no RTOS dependency. See Porting . Tested without hardware. Host unit tests run the driver against a model of the sensor's command interface. See Testing and CI . Where to go next ¶ Quickstart Wire the sensor, write the port, read oxygen in about 15 lines. API guide ¶ How to do the common jobs with the driver: identify the module, measure, read raw data, measure without blocking and handle errors. Every snippet on this page is compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/api_tasks.cpp , with Sensor standing for fdo2::Driver<MyUart> . The API reference lists every member. The shape of the API ¶ One fdo2::Driver<UartT> object per sensor. Each command is one call that sends the command, waits for the reply and returns a DriverResult<T> . Call Command Returns ReadVersion() #VERS VersionInfo : device id, channels, firmware, sensors ReadUniqueId() #IDNR uint64_t MeasureMoxy(timeout_ms) #MOXY MoxyReading : pO 2 , temperature, status MeasureMraw(timeout_ms) #MRAW MrawReading : the above plus dphi, signal, ambient light, pressure, humidity FlashLogo() #LOGO DriverResult<void> SendMeasure() , TryReadReplyLine() , ParseMoxyLine() , ParseMrawLine() , ParseVersionLine() any of the above The same exchange in two halves A DriverResult<T> has value , error and ok() , and converts to bool . The driver never throws and never allocates. Identify the module ¶ const auto version = sensor . ReadVersion (); // #VERS D N R S if ( ! version ) { std :: printf ( "#VERS failed: %s 
 " , fdo2 :: ToString ( version . error ). data ()); return false ; } std :: printf ( "device %" PRId32 ", firmware %.2f, sensors 0x%" PRIX32 " 
 " , version . value . device_id , fdo2 :: FirmwareRevisionToDouble ( version . value . firmware_revision ), static_cast < uint32_t > ( version . value . sensor_types )); // 15: O2, T, P, RH const auto id = sensor . ReadUniqueId (); // #IDNR N, unsigned 64-bit if ( id ) { std :: printf ( "unique id %" PRIu64 " 
 " , id . value ); } Call it once after power-up (wait kFdo2G2PowerUpSettleMs first). Device id 8 confirms an FDO2-G2; the firmware revision tells you whether the noise erratum applies. Measure oxygen ¶ const auto m = sensor . MeasureMoxy (); // #MOXY O T S if ( ! m ) { return false ; // Timeout, ProtocolError or DeviceError } if ( ! fdo2 :: MoxyStatusOkForOxygen ( m . value . status_u32 )) { return false ; // S > 1: O and T are or may be wrong } const double po2_hpa = m . value . p_o2_hpa ; // O x 10^-3 const double temp_c = m . value . temp_c ; // T x 10^-3 #MOXY is the shortest exchange: one measurement, three fields. A successful call means the module answered; the status check tells you whether the answer is a valid oxygen reading. A status of 1 (amplification reduced) is still valid. Read raw data and volume percent ¶ const auto r = sensor . MeasureMraw (); // #MRAW O T S D I A P H if ( ! r || ! fdo2 :: MoxyStatusOkForOxygen ( r . value . status_u32 )) { return false ; } // Valid when the gas at the membrane is at the pressure measured at the back of the housing. const double percent_o2 = fdo2 :: VolumePercentO2 ( r . value . p_o2_hpa , r . value . pressure_mbar ); // Optics check: keep signal + ambient light under about 2000 mV (shade the sensor otherwise). const bool too_bright = r . value . signal_intensity_mv + r . value . ambient_light_mv > 2000.0 ; #MRAW takes the same measurement and adds the raw optical values and the pressure and humidity inside the housing. Use it for diagnostics, for volume percent, or at a slower rate next to fast #MOXY reads, as the fdo2_sensor_demo example does. UART protocol lists every field and its unit. Measure without blocking ¶ MeasureMoxy() blocks for the whole measurement, up to about 150 ms. A loop that serves other devices can split the exchange: send the command, keep working, and pick up the reply when the UART has a complete line. // Start a measurement, do other work, collect the reply when the UART has it. class OxygenPoller { public : explicit OxygenPoller ( Sensor & sensor ) : sensor_ ( sensor ) {} void start () { pending_ = sensor_ . SendMeasure ( Sensor :: Measure :: Moxy ) == fdo2 :: DriverError :: None ; } // Call from your loop; true when a new reading was stored in `out`. bool poll ( fdo2 :: MoxyReading & out ) { char line [ 96 ]; if ( ! pending_ || sensor_ . TryReadReplyLine ( line , sizeof ( line )) != fdo2 :: DriverError :: None ) { return false ; // no complete line yet; you own the timeout } pending_ = false ; int32_t device_error = 0 ; const auto m = Sensor :: ParseMoxyLine ( line , & device_error ); if ( ! m || ! fdo2 :: MoxyStatusOkForOxygen ( m . value . status_u32 )) { return false ; } out = m . value ; return true ; } private : Sensor & sensor_ ; bool pending_ = false ; }; TryReadReplyLine() calls your port's read() with a timeout of 0, so the port must return a whole line or nothing ( Porting ). You own the timeout: if no reply arrives within about 300 ms, send the command again. Set timeouts ¶ sensor . SetMeasureTimeoutMs ( 400 ); // #MOXY / #MRAW: covers M = 3 or 4 (up to about 300 ms) sensor . SetLineTimeoutMs ( 400 ); // #VERS, #IDNR sensor . SetSlowCommandTimeoutMs ( 2000 ); // #LOGO: echoed after the ~1 s flash sequence const auto m = sensor . MeasureMoxy ( 1000 ); // or per call, in ms Timeout Default Used by Measurement 250 ms MeasureMoxy() , MeasureMraw() when called with 0 (the default argument) Line 400 ms ReadVersion() , ReadUniqueId() Slow command 12000 ms FlashLogo() : the echo comes after the LED has flashed, about 1 s The defaults fit the factory setting (M = 2, up to about 150 ms per measurement). A module set to M = 3 or 4 takes up to about 300 ms: raise the measurement timeout above that. Handle errors and status ¶ const auto m = sensor . MeasureMoxy (); switch ( m . error ) { case fdo2 :: DriverError :: None : break ; case fdo2 :: DriverError :: Timeout : // no reply: wiring, baud, power, still booting case fdo2 :: DriverError :: ProtocolError : // reply did not parse: noise, wrong baud, broadcast on case fdo2 :: DriverError :: CrcMismatch : // #CRCE 1 checksum wrong: corrupted in transit sensor . MeasureMoxy (); // the data sheet's advice: send the command again break ; case fdo2 :: DriverError :: DeviceError : // #ERRO E std :: printf ( "#ERRO %" PRId32 " 
 " , sensor . LastDeviceErrorCode ()); // -21, -22, -23: repeat; -26: unknown break ; default : std :: printf ( "%s 
 " , fdo2 :: ToString ( m . error ). data ()); break ; } if ( m && ( m . value . status_u32 & fdo2 :: moxy_status :: kWarnHumidityHigh ) != 0U ) { std :: printf ( "humidity in the housing above 90 %%RH 
 " ); } Signal Meaning What to do DriverError::Timeout No reply within the timeout Check wiring, baud rate, supply; wait 1 s after power-up DriverError::ProtocolError A reply that did not parse: wrong header or field count, a value that is not a number in range, no CR at the end Repeat the command; check the baud rate and broadcast mode DriverError::CrcMismatch With #CRCE 1 : the reply's checksum is wrong, or missing while SetCrcRequired(true) Repeat the command; see optional CRC DriverError::DeviceError #ERRO E LastDeviceErrorCode() ; error codes DriverError::BufferOverflow A reply longer than the line buffer Noise on RX, or broadcast replies running together MoxyStatusOkForOxygen(S) is false Status bits other than bit 0 set Do not use O and T ; see the status bits LastDeviceErrorCode() is reset to 0 at the start of every command, so read it right after the call that failed. Identify a sensor on a port ¶ return sensor . FlashLogo (). ok (); // status LED flashes 4 times, about 1 s: which sensor is on this port With several modules on several UARTs, FlashLogo() shows which connector belongs to which port. The module answers only after the flash sequence, so the call blocks for about 1 s, up to the slow-command timeout. docs.text: Architecture ¶ How the driver is put together: three layers, what each owns, and how one call reaches the sensor. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one fdo2::Driver object, whose public calls (listed from inc/fdo2_driver.hpp) send the FDO2-G2's ASCII commands and decode the replies into readings in hPa, degrees Celsius, mbar and %RH. The communication interface (UartInterface in inc/fdo2_uart_interface.hpp) is a CRTP base that forwards bytes to your class. The platform port is the only code you write: a class that writes a command, returns one reply line and flushes the receive buffer. Below it is the sensor. Drawn from: inc/fdo2_driver.hpp Driver public calls ; inc/fdo2_uart_interface.hpp UartInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . The three layers ¶ Layer Where You change it when Hardware-agnostic core : fdo2::Driver<UartT> inc/fdo2_driver.hpp , inc/fdo2_types.hpp Never, for a new board Communication interface : UartInterface<Derived> inc/fdo2_uart_interface.hpp Never Platform port : your class, three methods Your project Once per MCU or board ( Porting ) Everything above the port is the same on ESP32, STM32, a Linux host or the unit-test model. That is how the host tests run the real driver code without hardware. How one call reaches the sensor ¶ sequenceDiagram participant A as Application participant D as Driver participant P as Your port participant S as FDO2-G2 A->>D: MeasureMoxy() D->>P: flush_rx() D->>P: write(MOXY command, CR) P->>S: 6 bytes at 19200 baud S-->>P: MOXY 203456 17892 0, CR (after up to 150 ms) D->>P: read(buf, 511, 250 ms) P-->>D: one line, CR included D->>D: check and strip CRC suffix, split, check header, field count and every value D->>D: ERRO reply: DeviceError, code in LastDeviceErrorCode() D-->>A: result with MoxyReading: 203.456 hPa, 17.892 C, status 0 Why CRTP ¶ The interface is a class template parameter, not a virtual base class. The compiler sees your port's methods directly and inlines them; the driver has no vtable, allocates nothing and needs no RTTI. The cost is that the driver type names the port: fdo2::Driver<MyUart> . Code that has to work with several port types takes the driver as a template parameter too. Results instead of exceptions ¶ Every command returns DriverResult<T> : a value and an error ( DriverError ). It converts to bool , so if (!m) reads naturally, and fdo2::ToString(error) names the error for a log. An #ERRO reply from the module becomes DriverError::DeviceError , with the module's own code kept in LastDeviceErrorCode() until the next command. The status word S is not an error to the driver: a measurement with fault bits set still returns DriverError::None , because the module did answer. Checking S is your job, as the datasheet requires; the API guide shows how. Memory and timing ¶ The driver allocates nothing. A call uses under 1 KB of stack: the largest buffer is a 512-byte receive buffer, then the reply line and its tokens. A call blocks for at most the timeout you set, plus whatever your port's write() takes. docs.text: Changelog ¶ What changed in each release of the driver. Entries marked BREAKING need source changes in code that used the affected API. Unreleased ¶ Documentation ¶ The documentation site moved to the HardFOC MkDocs platform: new page set (quickstart, hardware, UART protocol, architecture, API guide, configuration, porting, examples, troubleshooting), the Doxygen API reference under /api/ , and every code sample compiled by the host build from tests/docs/ . docs.text: Hardware ¶ What to connect between your MCU and an FDO2-G2, with which UART settings, and the timing and power the module needs. All values here come from the FDO2-G2 datasheet (document version v5, 03/2026): specifications in section 2, the interface in section 4, the connector in section 7. Connector ¶ The module has a Molex 560020-0420 socket (four positions) on its back, next to the venting capillary. Directions are seen from the sensor. Pin Name Function 1 GND Ground 2 TXD Output: UART transmit, 3.0 V levels 3 RXD Input: UART receive, 3.0 V levels, 3.3 V tolerant 4 VCC Supply, 3.3 V to 5.0 V DC Connect MCU TX to pin 3 and MCU RX to pin 2. There are no other control pins: no reset, enable or interrupt line. The module is always on while VCC is present. 3.3 V maximum on RXD The UART runs at 3.0 V and its absolute maximum is 3.3 V. A 3.3 V MCU can drive RXD directly; a 5 V MCU needs a level shifter or a divider on its TX line. The 3.0 V high level on TXD is above the input-high threshold of most 3.3 V MCUs; check yours. UART settings ¶ Setting Value Baud rate 19200 after every power-up ( fdo2::kFdo2G2DefaultBaud ) Frame 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit Flow control None Command end CR ( 0x0D ), or CR LF Reply end CR only Other rates 1200 to 115200 with #BAUD , until the next power cycle; the driver does not send it The datasheet recommends 19200 for the highest reliability. At 19200 baud a #MOXY reply (about 25 characters) takes about 13 ms on the wire. Timing ¶ Event Time Power-up to first command about 1 s ( kFdo2G2PowerUpSettleMs = 1100 ms) Measurement, M = 0 to 2 (factory: 2) up to about 150 ms Measurement, M = 3 or 4 up to about 300 ms #CALO or #CAHI calibration up to 10 s Response time t 63 under 2 s Warm-up to full accuracy 3 min M is the flash duration mode set with #SETM (section 4.3); response time and warm-up are from section 2. The module measures only when asked (unless broadcast mode is on), so the measurement time is part of every #MOXY and #MRAW transaction: sequenceDiagram participant H as Host (driver) participant S as FDO2-G2 H->>H: flush_rx() H->>S: MOXY command, CR Note over S: temperature, ambient light, oxygen, housing sensors (up to 150 ms at M = 2) S-->>H: MOXY 203456 17892 0, CR H->>H: parse, scale: 203.456 hPa, 17.892 C, status 0 The driver's default measurement timeout is 250 ms. Raise it with SetMeasureTimeoutMs() if the module is set to M = 3 or 4 ( Configuration ). Power ¶ Parameter Value Supply voltage 3.3 V to 5.0 V DC Absolute maximum supply 5.5 V DC Current, standby / peak about 8 mA / 40 mA Energy per measurement about 1 to 2 mAs Do not interrupt the supply while the module writes its flash (after #CALO , #CAHI , #CRCE , #SETM or #BCST ): the datasheet warns that the flash can be corrupted. The driver sends none of these commands. Environment and mounting ¶ Parameter Value Operating temperature −10 °C to 60 °C Storage temperature −40 °C to 60 °C Internal pressure sensor range 300 mbar to 1100 mbar Maximum absolute / differential pressure 20 bar / 3 bar Humidity back side non-condensing; no dew point inside the membrane Mounting M16 x 1 thread; Ø 28.5 mm x 28 mm; 10.5 g Keep direct sunlight and strong lamps off the sensing membrane: ambient light shows up in the status word and in the #MRAW ambient-light field. The cross-sensitivity table (section 3) lists the gases that disturb or damage the sensor, NO 2 and Cl 2 among them. Errata ¶ Erratum Affects Status Increased noise at two module-specific temperatures, typically between 8 °C and 15 °C, each about ±0.1 °C wide Firmware 3.55 Fixed in firmware 3.57 with a hardware change (PCN-FDO2-G2-001) ReadVersion() returns the firmware revision: firmware_revision 357 is 3.57. Evaluation ¶ PyroScience sells the module with a USB adapter cable and the "Simple FDO2 Logger" software for Windows, which installs a virtual COM port to the module's UART. It is a quick way to see the module answer before you wire it to an MCU. The ESP32 examples run on an ESP32-S3 with the module on UART1. Reference documents ¶ Document What it is for FDO2-G2 datasheet Specifications, the UART command set, error codes, connector, errata PyroScience FDO2-G2 product page Accessories, newer datasheet revisions

docs.text: Installation ¶ Add the driver to a CMake or ESP-IDF project. It is a header-only C++17 library with no dependencies. Requirements ¶ A C++17 compiler. CI builds the tests with current GCC and Clang. CMake 3.16 or newer, for the CMake target. No RTOS, heap or exceptions: every call is noexcept and returns a DriverResult or a DriverError . Get the source ¶ A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to a version you chose: git submodule add https://github.com/hardfoc/hf-fdo2-driver.git external/hf-fdo2-driver git submodule update --init external/hf-fdo2-driver Only inc/ , cmake/ and CMakeLists.txt are needed to build. The examples have their own submodule ( examples/esp32/scripts ); you do not need it to use the driver. CMake ¶ add_subdirectory ( external/hf-fdo2-driver ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE hf::fdo2 ) hf::fdo2 is an INTERFACE target (alias of hf_fdo2 ). It carries the include directories, including the folder with the generated fdo2_version.h , and requires C++17 ( cxx_std_17 ). Option Default Effect HF_FDO2_ENABLE_WARNINGS OFF -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic on targets that link the driver HF_FDO2_BUILD_TESTS OFF Builds the host unit tests and documentation snippets in tests/ ( Testing and CI ) ESP-IDF ¶ The ESP-IDF component wrapper is examples/esp32/components/hf_fdo2/ . Copy that folder into your project's components/ (or point EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS at it) and set the HF_FDO2_ROOT cache variable to the driver checkout; the wrapper stops with a clear message when the path is wrong. Your component then declares REQUIRES hf_fdo2 . The wrapper itself requires the IDF driver component. docs.text: Porting ¶ Run the driver on a new MCU by writing one class: the UART interface. The driver never calls your SDK directly. It calls three methods (and an optional fourth) on a class you derive from fdo2::UartInterface<Self> (in inc/fdo2_uart_interface.hpp ). The base class uses CRTP: the calls are resolved at compile time, so there are no virtual functions, no vtable and nothing to allocate. Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one fdo2::Driver object, whose public calls (listed from inc/fdo2_driver.hpp) send the FDO2-G2's ASCII commands and decode the replies into readings in hPa, degrees Celsius, mbar and %RH. The communication interface (UartInterface in inc/fdo2_uart_interface.hpp) is a CRTP base that forwards bytes to your class. The platform port is the only code you write: a class that writes a command, returns one reply line and flushes the receive buffer. Below it is the sensor. Drawn from: inc/fdo2_driver.hpp Driver public calls ; inc/fdo2_uart_interface.hpp UartInterface ; figure module docs/diagrams/figures/driver-layers.py . What you implement ¶ Method Contract write(data, length) Send length bytes: one command, CR included. Return when they are queued or sent read(out, max, timeout_ms) Return one complete reply line, CR included, as a byte count; 0 if no whole line arrived within timeout_ms . With timeout_ms = 0, return only a line that is already complete flush_rx() Drop everything received so far, including a partial line delay_ms_impl(ms) Optional. Block for at least ms ; UartInterface::delay_ms() calls it, and does nothing without it The driver calls flush_rx() and then write() at the start of every command, and read() once per reply. docs.text: Run the driver on a new MCU by writing one class: the UART interface. The driver never calls your SDK directly. The platform port is the only code you write: a class that writes a command, returns one reply line and flushes the receive buffer. Below it is the sensor. docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Symptoms you may see while bringing up an FDO2-G2, their causes and the fix for each. Start with the DriverError of the failing call ( fdo2::ToString(result.error) ): Timeout points at wiring, baud rate or power; ProtocolError and CrcMismatch at what arrives on RX; DeviceError at the command, with the module's code in LastDeviceErrorCode() . No reply: every call returns Timeout ¶ Cause Check Fix TX and RX not crossed MCU TX must go to pin 3 (RXD), MCU RX to pin 2 (TXD) Swap the two lines, or the pins in your port Wrong baud rate The module runs at 19200 after every power-up Set 19200, 8N1, no flow control Module still booting First command less than 1 s after power-up Wait kFdo2G2PowerUpSettleMs (1100 ms) No supply or no common ground VCC at pin 4 between 3.3 V and 5.0 V, GND shared with the MCU Fix the harness; a 40 mA peak must not pull VCC below 3.3 V Port read() never returns a line A logic analyser shows the reply, but the call times out The port must return at the CR ( Porting ) Only FlashLogo() times out The LED flashes, but the #LOGO echo comes about 1 s later Keep SetSlowCommandTimeoutMs() above 1000 ms (default 12000 ms) Replies that do not parse: ProtocolError ¶ Cause Check Fix Broadcast mode left on #MRAW lines arrive without a command Send #BCST 0 once from a terminal; it is stored in flash Port returns partial lines Errors come and go, worse at low timeouts; a line without its CR is rejected Return one whole line, CR included, per read() Noise or a 5 V signal on RXD Garbled characters on a logic analyser Level-shift the MCU's TX; shorten or shield the cable The datasheet's advice for a garbled reply is to send the command again. Checksum errors: CrcMismatch ¶ The module has the CRC on ( #CRCE 1 ) and a reply's checksum did not match what arrived, or SetCrcRequired(true) is set and a reply came without one. A wrong checksum means the reply was corrupted on the line: send the command again, and look for noise or a level problem on RXD if it happens often. If every reply fails while the module's CRC is off, clear SetCrcRequired() ( UART protocol ). DeviceError after #ERRO ¶ Read LastDeviceErrorCode() right after the failing call. Codes -21, -22 and -23 are transmission errors: repeat the command. Code -26 means the module did not recognise the command. Any code not in the error table is potentially fatal: the datasheet says to replace the sensor and contact PyroScience. Status is not 0 or 1 ¶ The call succeeded but MoxyStatusOkForOxygen() is false : do not use the oxygen or temperature reading. Bit set Likely cause Fix 2 or 4 (signal or ambient light too high) Sunlight or a lamp on the sensing membrane Shade the sensor; check ambient_light_mv with #MRAW 1 or 3 (signal too low) Membrane damaged or contaminated, condensation Inspect the membrane; keep the dew point out of it 5 (temperature sensor) Sensor fault Replace the sensor 7 (humidity above 90 %RH, warning) Moisture reaching the housing through the back side Keep the back side dry and non-condensing 9 or 10 (pressure or humidity sensor) Housing sensor fault; pO 2 still valid MoxyStatusOkForOxygen() rejects these too; decide in your code whether to accept pO 2 The reading is plausible but off ¶ Symptom Cause Fix Drifts during the first minutes Warm-up: 3 min to full accuracy Discard readings for 3 min after power-up Volume percent wrong while pO 2 is right The membrane and the back of the housing are at different pressures Compute % O 2 from a pressure measured at the membrane Extra noise at one or two temperatures between 8 °C and 15 °C Firmware 3.55 erratum Firmware 3.57 fixes it; #SETM trades noise for drift ( Hardware ) Readings creep after exposure to solvents, NO 2 , Cl 2 or heat above 60 °C Cross-sensitivity or ageing See section 3 of the datasheet ; recalibrate or replace Calls take longer than the measurement ¶ Each MeasureMoxy() takes the full timeout (250 ms by default) instead of about 150 ms: the port's read() waits for max bytes or for the timeout instead of returning at the CR. Use the line-based port on Porting , or the ESP32 example port, which returns at the CR. Still stuck ¶ Open an issue with a capture of the UART traffic, the #VERS reply (firmware revision) and the driver version from fdo2::GetDriverVersion() .

docs.text: UART protocol ¶ The FDO2-G2's ASCII command protocol as the driver uses it: framing, commands, reply fields, status bits, error codes and the optional CRC. The source is section 4 of the FDO2-G2 datasheet (v5, 03/2026). Other PyroScience instruments use a different command set; this page and the driver apply to the FDO2-G2 only. Framing ¶ A command is a header ( # and capital letters, such as #MOXY ), optional values separated by spaces, and a CR ( 0x0D ) or CR LF. A reply that worked echoes the header, appends the requested values and ends with a single CR. A reply that failed is #ERRO E with a negative code E . Numbers are decimal ASCII in the range −2147483648 to 2147483647. The only exception is the #IDNR value, an unsigned 64-bit number of up to 20 digits. The driver sends the command, waits for one line, ignores a LF if one appears, and splits the line at spaces. It accepts a reply only if it ends with the CR, the header matches the command exactly, the number of values is the one listed below, and every value is a decimal number in its range: signed 32-bit, unsigned 32-bit for the status S , unsigned 64-bit for #IDNR . Anything else is DriverError::ProtocolError . Commands the driver sends ¶ Command Reply Driver call #VERS #VERS D N R S ReadVersion() #IDNR #IDNR N ReadUniqueId() #MOXY #MOXY O T S MeasureMoxy() , or SendMeasure(Measure::Moxy) #MRAW #MRAW O T S D I A P H MeasureMraw() , or SendMeasure(Measure::Mraw) #LOGO #LOGO FlashLogo() : the status LED flashes 4 times, about 1 s, then the echo arrives #VERS reports D = 8 for every FDO2-G2, N = 1 oxygen channel, the firmware revision as R = 357 for 3.57, and S, a bit mask of the sensors present (bit 0 oxygen, bit 1 temperature, bit 2 pressure, bit 3 humidity; 15 means all). The unique id from #IDNR is not the serial number printed on the device. Reply fields ¶ Every field is a signed 32-bit integer, except the status S , which is unsigned. The driver keeps the raw value and adds the scaled one. Field Raw unit Scaled member Typical range O oxygen partial pressure 10 −3 hPa p_o2_hpa 0 to 210 hPa in air T sensor temperature m°C temp_c 0 °C to 50 °C S status bits status_u32 0 or 1 in normal operation D phase shift dphi m° dphi_deg 5° to 60° I signal intensity µV signal_intensity_mv 100 mV to 500 mV A ambient light µV ambient_light_mv 0 to about 100 mV P pressure at the back of the housing µbar pressure_mbar 900 mbar to 1100 mbar H humidity inside the housing m%RH rh_in_housing_pct 10 %RH to 90 %RH O , T and S come with both #MOXY and #MRAW ; the rest only with #MRAW . Every scaled member is the raw value times 10 −3 . Two rules from the datasheet for the #MRAW values: Signal and ambient light. Keep I + A under about 2000 mV. Above it the detector can saturate; shade the sensor. Compare signal intensities only at similar oxygen levels: about 200 mV to 400 mV is typical at 200 hPa and room temperature. Volume percent. When the gas at the membrane is at the same pressure as the back of the housing, % O 2 = 100 x pO 2 / P. fdo2::VolumePercentO2(p_o2_hpa, pressure_mbar) computes it (1 mbar = 1 hPa) and returns 0 for a pressure of zero or below. Status bits ¶ Bit Constant in fdo2::moxy_status Meaning 0 kWarnAutoAmpReduced Warning: amplification reduced to avoid saturation; the reading is valid 1 kFatalSignalTooLow Fatal: oxygen signal below 20 mV 2 kFatalSignalTooHigh Fatal: oxygen signal or ambient light too high 3 kFatalRefTooLow Fatal: reference signal below 20 mV 4 kFatalRefTooHigh Fatal: reference signal or ambient light above 2400 mV 5 kFatalTempSensor Fatal: temperature sensor failure 7 kWarnHumidityHigh Warning: humidity in the housing above 90 %RH 9 kErrPressureSensor Error: housing pressure sensor failure; pO 2 not affected 10 kErrHumiditySensor Error: housing humidity sensor failure; pO 2 not affected Bits 6 and 8 are reserved. The datasheet's rule: under normal operation S is 0 or 1; any other value means O and T are or can be wrong, and the user must check S on every measurement. fdo2::MoxyStatusOkForOxygen(S) is that rule. Error codes ¶ A command that failed returns #ERRO E . The driver turns it into DriverError::DeviceError and keeps E in LastDeviceErrorCode() . E Type Meaning and what to do -1 General A non-specific error -21 UART parse The command did not parse; repeat it -22 UART receive The command was not received correctly (not ready, bad terminator); repeat it -23 UART header The header has characters other than A to Z; repeat it -26 UART request The header matches no supported command -60 Invalid calibration A calibration was out of range and was discarded Any other code is potentially fatal: the datasheet says to replace the sensor and contact PyroScience. Optional CRC ¶ #CRCE 1 makes the module end every reply with a colon, a space and a CRC-16 as decimal ASCII before the CR: #MOXY 203456 17892 0: 43291 , then CR. The CRC is the MODBUS one (CRC-16-IBM: reflected polynomial 0xA001 , initial value 0xFFFF , no final XOR) over every byte from the start of the reply up to, not including, the colon, spaces included. The setting is stored in flash and survives a power cycle. The driver checks the CRC of every reply that carries one, #ERRO replies included, and removes the suffix before it parses the reply. A wrong checksum returns DriverError::CrcMismatch ; a colon not followed by a number from 0 to 65535 returns ProtocolError . Call SetCrcRequired(true) on a module with the CRC on to reject replies that arrive without it. The driver never sends #CRCE . Without the CRC, the datasheet's first-level check is the echo of the command header, which the driver does compare. Commands the driver does not send ¶ Command What it does Why the driver leaves it out #CALO , #CAHI P Two-point calibration at 0 % and at P ; discards the factory calibration Writes flash; up to 10 s; needs a calibration gas #SETM M Flash duration mode 0 (lowest drift) to 4 (lowest noise); default 2 Writes flash #BCST T Broadcast #MRAW replies every T ms (100 to 10000) Writes flash; interleaves with command replies #CRCE K CRC on or off Writes flash #BAUD R Baud rate until the next power cycle Not implemented #RDUM , #WRUM Read and write 64 words of user memory Not implemented; #WRUM writes flash The module tolerates about 20,000 flash cycles, and an interrupted flash write can corrupt it. Send these commands from a service tool with a stable supply, not from production firmware. If a module arrives with broadcast mode on, send #BCST 0 once: its broadcasts otherwise interrupt the driver's replies. CI runs hardfoc-docs figures --check and fails when a committed figure no longer matches the code. Each figure below lists the files it is drawn from. Three layers, one of them yours ¶ Three layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources From top to bottom. Your application talks to one fdo2::Driver object, whose public calls (listed from inc/fdo2_driver.hpp) send the FDO2-G2's ASCII commands and decode the replies into readings in hPa, degrees Celsius, mbar and %RH. The communication interface (UartInterface in inc/fdo2_uart_interface.hpp) is a CRTP base that forwards bytes to your class. The platform port is the only code you write: a class that writes a command, returns one reply line and flushes the receive buffer. Below it is the sensor.
